posts.text: AI does not automatically reduce costs. It can lower operational expenses, automate repetitive work, speed up decisions, and help teams do more with fewer manual steps. But enterprise AI comes with a cost structure that is easy to underestimate. Every prompt consumes tokens. Every response uses inference capacity. Every agent workflow may trigger multiple model calls, tools, APIs, retrieval steps, and databases. Then add GPU infrastructure, vector storage, observability, security, evaluation, integration, and engineering time. Suddenly, “AI will save us money” becomes a much more complicated equation. The real question is not: “Can AI reduce costs?” It is: “Can this AI system create more business value than it costs to operate?” That means enterprises need to measure more than model accuracy. They need to track: → Cost per task → Tokens per workflow → Cost per successful outcome → Infrastructure utilization → Human hours saved → Automation rate → Error and retry costs → Revenue or productivity impact And this becomes even more important with AI agents. An agent might make 10, 20, or 50 calls to complete what looks like one simple request. Enterprise AI needs FinOps thinking from day one. Because the goal is not to build the smartest AI system. The goal is to build an AI system whose economics actually make sense at scale. ROI should be designed into the architecture, not calculated after deployment.

posts.text: Give me 2 minutes. I’ll show you what really sits behind ChatGPT. What users see is a simple chat window. What makes it work is an entire AI stack, with every layer building on the one below it. It starts with data: raw facts, observations, documents, images, and signals collected from the real world. Then comes infrastructure: the compute, storage, networks, and platforms required to train and run AI systems. Algorithms provide the methods that identify patterns within that data. Models learn those patterns and use them to generate predictions or decisions. Machine learning makes this possible by allowing systems to learn from examples instead of relying only on fixed rules. Deep learning takes it further through multilayer neural networks capable of understanding complex relationships across language, images, audio, and more. Generative AI uses those capabilities to create entirely new outputs, including text, code, images, video, and audio. Finally, ChatGPT and other AI tools sit at the application layer, where people interact with the underlying intelligence. The important point is that ChatGPT is one application within a much deeper system. Real AI value does not come from a model working alone. It comes from quality data, scalable infrastructure, suitable algorithms, reliable models, and useful applications working together. More data also does not automatically produce better AI. Better data, stronger models, and thoughtful system design matter far more. AI becomes easier to understand when you stop viewing it as magic and start viewing it as a connected system. Understand the stack, and you understand where AI’s real value comes from.

posts.text: Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent: Which One Do You Actually Need? Everyone wants to build a team of AI agents. Almost nobody checks if they need one. SINGLE-AGENT Try Gamma (try.gamma.app/rxvp3qlex13h) World’s #1 AI-Powered Presentation Generator Visit ➡️ try.gamma.app/rxvp3qlex13h One agent runs the whole job — takes the goal, gathers context, plans, executes, checks its own work, delivers one answer. Use it when: the task has one clear objective, one agent can hold all the context, it's calling a few tools (not dozens), steps happen in order, and speed/cost matter more than depth. MULTI-AGENT A coordinator splits the goal among specialists (researcher, analyst, writer, critic, etc.) who work in parallel/sequence, then merges their output. Use it when: subtasks need genuinely different skills, work can run in parallel, a second opinion adds real value, and each stage needs its own check. The catch: every extra agent is another handoff — another place for context to drop, another cost, another thing to debug when it breaks. More agents ≠ more intelligence; it's more surface area for silent failure. Rule of thumb: Single-agent = one capable generalist. Multi-agent = a team, and a team needs a manager — that's you. Before your next architecture call, ask: "What breaks today if this stays one agent?" If no one has a specific answer, you don't need a team — you need a sharper single agent.

posts.text: Enterprise AI has split into two camps. One says the priority is context: better data, clearer definitions, a real understanding of the business. The other says it’s control: visibility, ownership and the ability to audit what an agent did and why. Both are right. Neither is sufficient alone. Context without control is exposure. Control without context is paralysis. I’ve seen enterprises spend a year getting their definitions right, but have no idea which agents are using them, bypassing them or relying on context that went stale months ago. I’ve also seen the reverse: a fully auditable agent with clear lineage and ownership, confidently acting on data nobody validated. Control can tell you who’s accountable for the failure. It doesn’t prevent it. Enterprise AI needs context and control built as one system, not two projects running on parallel tracks. I wrote more about why in my latest blog. posts.text: Most people misunderstand AI governance. This is the simplest way to finally see it clearly. AI governance is not a policy. It is a pipeline. And the simplest way to understand it is with a kid, a backpack, and ten teachers. Every record moves through the system the same way a kid moves through a school. The kid is the record. The backpack is the metadata. The teachers are the enforcement rules. The classrooms are the pipeline stages. The kid carries the backpack everywhere. Inside the backpack are governance tags like privacy category, classification level, jurisdiction, retention period, risk tier, and transparency requirement. The teachers walk beside the kid. At every classroom door, the teachers check the backpack. Only the rules that matter speak. Privacy speaks when the record is sensitive. Global transfer speaks when the record has a border restriction. Retention speaks when the record has a time limit. Risk speaks when the record is high risk. The governance metadata choose the rules. The enforcement engine activates the rules. This is governance. This is the governed record. This is the pipeline. If your AI system cannot prove that metadata and enforcement rules travel with every record and activate at every stage, you do not have governance. You have exposure. Governance is the proof. Without proof, there is no trust.

posts.text: End-to-End Generative AI Production Architecture Building an AI model is the easy part. The real engineering challenge starts when you need to make it reliable, scalable, secure, observable, and production-ready. A real-world GenAI application is much more than: User → LLM → Response It looks more like: User → Frontend → API/Gateway → AI Orchestrator → RAG + Tools + Agents → LLM → Response 1️⃣ Application Layer The application layer handles the user experience, frontend, API gateway, orchestration, and final response. The orchestrator coordinates workflows, manages context, retrieves knowledge, and decides when to call tools or agents. 2️⃣ Data + RAG Layer Your AI is only as useful as the knowledge it can access. Data can come from: 📄 PDFs & documents 🌐 Websites 🗄️ Databases 🔌 APIs ☁️ Cloud storage A typical RAG pipeline is: Ingest → Extract → Chunk → Embed → Store → Retrieve Vector stores such as Pinecone, FAISS, and Chroma can retrieve relevant context before the LLM generates a response. 3️⃣ Agentic AI Layer This is where applications move beyond simple chat. Frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen can enable: → Planning → Reasoning → Tool calling → Multi-step execution → Context management → Multi-agent workflows 4️⃣ Model Layer Applications can connect to models such as GPT, Claude, Llama, and Mistral through platforms including OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and AWS Bedrock. Models can handle tasks such as: → Reasoning → Summarization → Code generation → Function calling → Content generation 5️⃣ Cloud Infrastructure Production AI needs more than a model. You also need: Compute + Storage + Databases + Cache + Networking + Secrets Common platforms include AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. 6️⃣ DevOps & CI/CD A typical deployment pipeline: Git → Build → Test → Docker → Registry → Deploy → Monitor This enables repeatable deployments, faster releases, and easier scaling. 7️⃣ Observability + Security A production AI system must answer: Is it working? How fast is it? How much does it cost? Why did it fail? Is it secure? That’s where logging, tracing, Prometheus/Grafana, authentication, RBAC, encryption, rate limiting, guardrails, and evaluation become critical. The complete picture: User → Frontend → API/Gateway → AI Orchestrator → RAG + Tools + Agents → LLM → Response And around all of it: Cloud + CI/CD + Security + Monitoring + Evaluation That’s the difference between an AI demo and a production AI platform. The biggest mistake is focusing only on the LLM. Production GenAI is an engineering system — not just a model. posts.text: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recently called cybersecurity AI’s “next blockbuster app.” I think there is a much broader shift behind that statement. As enterprises move from AI assistants to agents capable of accessing data, calling APIs, writing code and executing business processes, cybersecurity is becoming part of the AI operating model itself. Three implications stand out to me: 1. AI is scaling both sides of cybersecurity. Attackers can automate reconnaissance, phishing, vulnerability discovery and social engineering. Defenders can increasingly automate detection, investigation and response. The advantage will not necessarily belong to whoever deploys the most security tools. It will belong to organizations that can integrate security, AI and automation into a coherent operating model. 2. Securing AI is becoming a business capability. An enterprise AI agent with access to applications, data and workflows starts to resemble a new type of privileged digital worker. That raises very practical questions: What identity does the agent operate under? What data can it access? Which tools can it invoke? Who authorizes its actions? How are those actions monitored, governed and audited? These are no longer only AI governance questions. They are cybersecurity and enterprise architecture questions. 3. The attack surface is expanding faster than many organizations realize. Every agent, model endpoint, API, tool connection, vector database, open-source component and machine identity introduces another potential control point. This is why I believe the next phase of enterprise AI will increasingly bring together AI governance, cybersecurity, identity, automation and observability rather than treating them as separate disciplines. The next AI race will not simply be about who has the most powerful models. It will be about who can deploy increasingly autonomous intelligence at scale — while maintaining security, governance and control. That may become one of the defining enterprise capabilities of the agentic era. hashtag #Cybersecurity hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #AIGovernance hashtag #EnterpriseAI hashtag #AISecurity hashtag #DigitalTrust https://lnkd.in/dqqbeYkG

posts.text: Most ERP vendors are bolting AI onto existing software. If the AI can be removed and the ERP still works exactly the same way, it isn’t AI-native. It’s an add-on. NetSuite is building NetSuite Next around the opposite premise: intelligence embedded into how the system operates, not bolted onto the interface. At The Six Five Summit: AI Unleashed 2026, Keith Kirkpatrick and Nick Patience welcomed Brian Chess, Senior Vice President of AI, Product, and Technology at Oracle NetSuite, to explain what it takes to make ERP truly AI-native. The central engineering challenge wasn’t building a better chatbot. It was giving AI direct access to the application layer, allowing it to invoke NetSuite’s existing functionality, business rules, and workflows instead of inventing new solutions the business never requested. Key Insights: 🔹 AI-native is a functional test, not a marketing label. 🔹 NetSuite's anomaly detection flags irregular transactions and surfaces context, but leaves correction to a human until that trust is earned. 🔹 Agent design is still being tested at the specialization level. 🔹 Connecting outside AI tools is changing user behavior, not just output. 🔹 Accountability doesn't transfer to the AI. Chess is direct on this point: humans keep ownership of the outcome even as automation absorbs more of the work needed to reach it. The bigger signal here is about design philosophy. NetSuite's bet is that AI-native ERP wins by embedding intelligence into how the system already operates, not by adding a layer on top. Watch the full conversation: https://lnkd.in/d2-WCDxC

posts.text: Heading into 2026, the safe bet was that enterprise AI would consolidate around a handful of generalist platforms. Our data shows the opposite. Companies buying AI now work with 5.4 vendors on average, and 61% run five or more. Rather than standardize on a single platform, companies are accumulating vendors and a portfolio is emerging whether it was planned or not. That's a new kind of problem for procurement. Capabilities are overlapping across vendors, and AI pricing models seem to change every few months. And as the request queue keeps growing, teams have to govern what's already in the door and keep pace with a business that wants more. Here’s my bet. The next stage of enterprise AI will be less about adopting it and more about managing it: deciding where it belongs, which tools to trust, and when to add, replace, or retire applications. What do you think will be the hardest part of managing AI at enterprise scale?

posts.text: Most boards are asking, “How do we use AI?” The better question is: “How do we govern AI when we can’t even see everything it is doing?” AI governance is no longer an IT problem. It is a boardroom responsibility. Because once AI starts making decisions, accessing data, interacting with customers, or acting through agents, the risk changes completely. A board needs answers to questions like: → Who owns each AI system? → What data can it access? → What permissions does it have? → How are we monitoring its actions? → Can we stop it quickly if something goes wrong? → Are our vendors actually accountable? → Can we prove our controls work? This is where many organizations are still behind. They have AI policies. But policies sitting in a document don’t protect an organization. Operational controls do. A stronger AI governance model connects: 1. Strategic exposure Understand business, legal, operational and reputational risks before procurement. 2. Execution & controls Continuously monitor AI systems, assess risks, test security and maintain human oversight. 3. Compliance reality Map regulations and contracts to the systems actually being deployed. And most importantly: Make accountability visible. The board should own the strategic direction. The CISO should own the technical controls. The legal team should own regulatory and third-party exposure. But none of them can operate in isolation. Because AI risk doesn’t respect organizational boundaries. The real test isn’t: “Do we have an AI policy?” It’s: “Can we confidently explain what our AI is doing, where our data is going, who is accountable, and what happens when something goes wrong?” If the answer is no, you don’t have AI governance yet. You have AI assumptions. And assumptions are a dangerous foundation for the systems that will increasingly run your business. Save this framework. Your next AI governance conversation should start here. P.S. If your board asked you tomorrow, “Show me how we govern AI,” could you answer in 5 minutes?

posts.text: The Forward Outcome Delivery Model for IT Companies. IT services companie's role is changing from delivering technology to being accountable for business outcomes; as clients increasingly expect them to understand the business problem, diagnose what is holding performance back, define the value to be created & shape right solution with AI. This requires a different delivery model. The proposed Forward Outcome Delivery Model extends Palantir’s Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) model further by adding deep industry, domain & operating knowledge with stronger business & consultative roles before engineering begins. It will be extremely important when redesigning workflows, value chains & setting measurable business outcomes becomes as critical as adopting / integrating AI. Forward Outcome Delivery Model: It aims to create a layer by combining experienced domain & industry professionals with AI native engineering teams. It's a two-layer, outcome-led delivery model. The first roles converts a business problem into an outcome architecture; the second converts that architecture into a working solution. 1. Forward Outcome Architects Senior, business-facing roles deployed before the technology team with a 15+ years of domain, industry or operating experience, strengthened with consultative and AI-era problem-solving capabilities. Responsibilities Understand the business problem, operating context & constraints>Diagnose root causes, value leakages>Define the desired business outcomes, measurable success criteria>Identify where AI, data, process redesign & technology can create value> Translate the problem into a clear Value & Outcome Charter. 2. Forward Development Engineers A multidisciplinary engineering team that converts the charter into the solution with AI, Data, Software Engineering, Agentic Systems, integration & product engineering skills. Responsibilities Convert outcome requirements into solution architecture>Build AI, data, application & agentic components>Integrate into existing enterprise systems & workflows with orchestrated human & AI work>Deliver agreed value & outcome measures. Advantages of this model For the client, it improves solution relevance & reduces the risk of technically successful projects with weak business outcomes. For the IT company, it moves the engagement upstream to improve differentiation, deal size, strategic relevance, margins & long-term client relationships. Instead of allowing institutional knowledge of middle-management to disappear, companies can re-skill the strongest of these professionals into Forward Outcome Architects & convert a potential redundancy problem into a new consultative capability & competitive advantage. This can become a simple infusion of business-to-engineering translation layer, quikly introduced without much disturbance & as input for restructuring the business for AI-Era Target Operating Model. posts.text: 𝟖𝟖% 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. That's Gartner's 2026 number. But everyone is still building agents. Here are 7 failure modes I see repeatedly: 𝟏. 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐄𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐫𝐬: Per-step reliability of 95% sounds good, but a 10-step task succeeds only 60% of the time. Your "99% accurate" agent fails 40% of the time in production. 𝟐. 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐑𝐨𝐭: Accuracy degrades as the transcript grows, and this happens well before you hit context window limits. Long-running agents get dumber over time. 𝟑. 𝐌𝐚𝐥𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬: Free-text generation isn't constrained to your API schema, so agents invent arguments that don't exist. They call functions that were deprecated last week. 𝟒. 𝐑𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬: No hard stop on retries means infinite loops, and one misconfigured workflow can burn $3,000 in API calls. You find out when the invoice arrives, not when it happens. 𝟓. 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: Untrusted input can hijack the agent's behavior, so a customer email changes what it does. A webpage redirects it to execute something else. 𝟔. 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐕𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐬: Demos are one happy-path run you retried until it looked good, but production is thousands of unattended runs with a non-deterministic model. Real systems charge cards and write rows. 𝟕. 𝐍𝐨 𝐎𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: You can see the request and response, but everything in between is opaque. When it breaks, you have no traces and no way to debug. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐧𝐮𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫: 78% of enterprises have agent pilots & 14% have scaled one successfully. The gap isn't model quality. It's reliability engineering. posts.text: Where does Agentic AI outperform traditional automation? Look for work that requires complex decision-making, rules that frequently change, or heavy use of unstructured data. In these scenarios, agents can interpret context, evaluate exceptions, adapt to new information, and manage multi-step workflows better than basic automation, which eventually finds a way to get tripped up. But choosing the right use case is only the beginning. Teams also need clearly defined outcomes, guardrails, human oversight, and evaluation criteria to move from an impressive demo to a reliable enterprise solution.
